violations.message: expected real return 1.79% is below the CPI + 3.0% target
ex-ante tracking error 9.30% exceeds the 6.0% budget vs. 60/40 equity-bond benchmark

body.rationale: This is the diversifier doing its §3.4 job, and the result is informative rather than a recommendation. The method maximises tracking variance to the centroid of every other proposal, subject to a Sharpe floor of 75% of the maximum-Sharpe portfolio. Most of the roster, after the cash-like exclusion for risk-only methods, sits in a broad equity-bond-real mix. The point furthest from that centroid is the cash-like end of the universe, so the optimiser went there. It surfaces two things the other proposals do not. First, the Sharpe floor is a ratio. It is scale-invariant, so a portfolio of near-riskless assets clears it easily, because the small excess return (roughly 0.7%, implied by Sharpe 0.60 at 1.17% volatility) is divided by a tiny volatility. The floor therefore does not stop the optimiser from leaving the IPS risk band, and the CIO should know that when reading any proposal that cites a high Sharpe. Second, it defines the opposite pole of the proposal set, a no-risk-asset position. That gives the ensemble a measure of how far the other candidates sit from pure carry, and how much of their expected return is compensation for bearing risk. Judged against the IPS this portfolio fails outright. It misses the CPI+3% real-return target, sits far below the 8-12% volatility band, and its 9.30% tracking error breaches the 6% budget. The IPS is ratified, so these are real breaches. I do not argue for holding it. Any contribution to the ensemble is as a small ballast or de-risking sleeve. If the CIO wants to hold a higher-conviction, higher-volatility candidate such as a tuned max-Sharpe or equity-tilted proposal, a small allocation here lowers drawdown and tracking error, at the cost of ensemble return. Because the ensemble must stay above the 8% volatility floor, the usable weight is small.
body.notes: Tracking error to the centroid of the other 14 proposals: 7.24%. Key assumption: The other proposals form a meaningful centroid, and that a portfolio far from it, with a Sharpe above 75% of the maximum, surfaces useful ideas. This requires the judged CMAs for cash-like assets, and hence the risk-free spread, to be accurate enough that a roughly 0.7% excess return over tiny volatility is a real edge. Main weakness: The Sharpe of 0.60 is a ratio of a very small excess return to a very small volatility, so it is extremely sensitive to CMA error on cash and short-Treasury returns and to the risk-free rate. A shift of a few tenths of a percentage point in those CMAs could take the portfolio below the floor or make it look far better. The headline Sharpe is also not comparable with that of portfolios that carry real risk. The portfolio fails three hard IPS limits: expected real return 1.79% against a CPI+3% target, volatility 1.17% against the 8-12% band, and tracking error 9.30% against the 6% budget. It is also nearly a single exposure (1.9 effective assets), has no equity or real-asset growth engine, and is exposed to reinvestment-rate and inflation risk. Preferred when: Use it as a diagnostic and as a candidate defensive sleeve, not as a standalone choice. It is most useful when the CIO faces a high-volatility or concentrated proposal that needs a lower-risk offset, when peer reviewers suspect the other methods cluster around the same equity-bond exposure, or when the regime turns defensive (late-cycle or contraction) and the case for holding cash-like ballast strengthens. In the current expansion regime the case is weaker, since the opportunity cost of avoiding risk assets is highest. Invalidated if: It is the wrong choice if the ensemble needs return, since the portfolio cannot meet the CPI+3% target on its own and a meaningful weight would pull the ensemble below the 8% volatility floor. It is also wrong if the CMAs for cash-like assets are overstated, or if the risk-free spread is smaller than implied, so that the Sharpe floor was only cleared by estimation error. It is further undermined if the other proposals are not clustered, so that the centroid is not informative, or if inflation or rate-cut risk makes cash-like assets lose real value over the horizon.
